catalog_quote: Welmers 1976 p.29: "3.1. Vai is a discrete-level tone language with two tones. Throughout a phrase or sentence, there is no appreciable downdrift conditioned by a low tone between two high tones. ... 3.2. A single vowel or syllabic nasal may have a single tone ... In forms with two syllables or two immediately successive vowels, any possible sequence of the two tones may occur: high-high, low-low, high-low, low-high." p.36: "4.1. The tones of Vai as described above are heard in isolated words and phrases, and without appreciable difference in complete declarative sentences and in question-word questions." Koelle 1854 p.43: "I. The accent in all isolated words lies on the first syllable; e. g. dende, firi, anu; Doaru, koari, mdanu; barawara. ... In foreign words, however, the accent is generally suffered to remain unchanged; e.g. Mondovia, Setana, dsahanama." p.44: "II. In a sentence,…

audit.reasoning: The coding 'tonal' (two discrete level tones, all four disyllabic sequences contrastive, grammatical tone, no stress/accent mentioned) rests on Welmers 1976, the standard and only modern reference grammar of Vai, with dedicated Tones and Intonations chapters; all three Welmers quotations and the Koelle 1854 historical 'accent' quotations were confirmed verbatim at the stated pages in the held files. Glottolog's 68-item bibliography and CrossRef contain no later phonology, prosody or instrumental study of Vai; the only later linguistic work found (Tröbs 2014, Kastenholz 2019 dictionary) follows Welmers' tonal analysis and is silent on stress. Nothing suggests a recode.
